name: Phosphatidic acid

card.summary: A membrane lipid sold as a pre-workout supplement because it signals to mTOR in cells; direct human evidence for added muscle is small and thin.
card.note: Cell-biology findings on mTOR are well established; evidence that oral supplements add muscle in people rests on very few small trials.

quick.overview:
Phosphatidic acid (PA) is a naturally occurring phospholipid found in every cell membrane. It is also sold as an over-the-counter supplement marketed to people who lift weights, on the premise that it activates the mTOR growth pathway.

The cell-biology link between PA and mTOR is well documented. Whether swallowing PA raises PA levels in muscle, and whether that produces extra muscle in people, has been tested in only a few small trials, and the ClinicalTrials.gov registrations for such studies are small.
quick.mechanism: In cell experiments, PA binds a domain of the mTOR protein and is needed for mitogen-driven activation of mTOR signaling, which regulates protein synthesis and cell growth [1][2]. Supplement proponents extrapolate from this to muscle growth after resistance training. Other work shows mTORC1 controls the location of lipin 1, an enzyme that processes PA [3].
quick.risks: PA is sold as a dietary supplement in the US, where supplements are regulated as foods and manufacturers are responsible for confirming safety [4]. Published safety data for supplemental PA in healthy lifters are limited. Because it is a general cell-signaling lipid, its role in other tissues has been studied mainly in laboratory research.

lead: Phosphatidic acid (PA) is the simplest glycerophospholipid: a glycerol backbone carrying two fatty acid chains and a phosphate group. It is a precursor for other membrane lipids and also acts as a signaling molecule inside cells [5][6].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities PA is discussed as an over-the-counter, mTOR-activating supplement taken around resistance training with the aim of adding muscle size and strength. The marketing rationale draws on a 2001 Science paper reporting that PA binds mTOR and is required for its activation in cultured cells [1].

The cell-level mechanism is well characterised, but evidence that oral PA supplements increase muscle in humans is limited to a small number of short trials, and published independent replication is sparse.

paras: PA is made in cells by several routes: acylation of lysophosphatidic acid, cleavage of phosphatidylcholine by phospholipase D, and phosphorylation of diacylglycerol by diacylglycerol kinase. It is broken down to diacylglycerol or lysophosphatidic acid [5][6].

Its small headgroup shapes membrane curvature, and it recruits and regulates proteins, including mTOR, Raf1, protein kinase C epsilon and several ion channels [5][6]. Researchers still debate how much PA signals directly versus acting mainly as a precursor to diacylglycerol, and different fatty-acid species may have different activities [5].

The 2001 study reported that mitogen stimulation raised phospholipase D-dependent PA in cells, that this PA was required to activate mTOR effectors, and that PA interacted directly with the mTOR domain targeted by the drug rapamycin [1]. A 2011 Cell paper showed mTOR complex 1 in turn regulates the lipid-processing enzyme lipin 1, which converts PA to diacylglycerol, linking mTOR to lipid synthesis [2].

Resistance training activates mTORC1 signaling and muscle protein synthesis, which is the basis of the hypothesis that supplying PA could amplify that response [7]. Encyclopedia entries on the compound describe its cellular roles but do not address oral supplementation [5][6].

Few registered human trials exist. One completed trial, "Determining the Muscle Anabolic Properties of Phosphatidic Acid," enrolled 16 participants with sarcopenia as a focus condition (started 2015) [8]. A second registration, "Effects of Phosphatidic Acid on Strength and Hypertrophy," planned 45 participants (started 2020) and its status is listed as unknown [9]. The registration records do not report results in the material reviewed, so the size of any effect is not established here.
Other registered trials of related compounds (for example, a PA-derived lipid under study for knee osteoarthritis) address different conditions and are not evidence for muscle gain.

timeline.event: Science paper identifies PA as a component of mitogenic mTOR signaling [1].
Cell paper links mTORC1 to lipin 1 (a PA phosphatase) and the SREBP lipid pathway [2].
A small trial of PA's muscle-anabolic properties begins [8].

lore.intro: PA appears in supplement marketing as an "mTOR activator" for lifters; no forum material is cited here, so the claims below reflect how products are positioned rather than specific forum threads.

claims.claim: Taking PA around training activates mTOR and adds extra muscle.
claims.believers: Proponents point to the cell studies showing PA binds and activates mTOR and reason that supplying more PA amplifies the post-workout growth signal [1].
claims.experts: The cell-level mechanism is published [1][2], but only a few small human trials have been registered and detailed outcome data are limited [8][9].
